text_blocks.snippet: Swollen ankles are often a sign of problems with the heart, kidneys, or liver. These organs play crucial roles in regulating fluid balance within the body, and when they are not functioning properly, fluid can accumulate in the lower extremities, leading to swelling.

list.title: Heart Failure:
list.snippet: The heart's inability to pump blood effectively can cause a buildup of fluid in the body, leading to edema (swelling) in the ankles and feet.

list.title: Kidney Disease:
list.snippet: Impaired kidney function can result in the body retaining excess fluid and sodium, causing swelling in the ankles and feet.

list.title: Liver Disease:
list.snippet: Liver problems, especially cirrhosis, can affect the production of proteins like albumin, which help keep fluid inside blood vessels. This can lead to fluid leaking into surrounding tissues and causing swelling in the legs and ankles.

text_blocks.snippet: Other potential causes of swollen ankles include:

list.snippet: Venous insufficiency: Weak or damaged valves in the leg veins can cause blood to pool in the lower legs, leading to swelling.
Lymphedema: Disruption of the lymphatic system, which helps remove excess fluid from tissues, can cause swelling.
Blood clots: Blood clots in the legs can impede blood flow and cause swelling.
Pregnancy: Swelling is common during pregnancy due to hormonal changes and increased blood volume.
Medications: Certain medications can have swelling as a side effect.
Injuries: Ankle injuries can cause swelling due to inflammation and fluid buildup.

text_blocks.snippet: If you experience persistent or severe ankle swelling, it's important to consult with a healthcare professional to determine the underlying cause and receive appropriate treatment.

related_questions.question: When should I be concerned about swollen feet and ankles?

text_blocks.snippet: You should be concerned about swollen feet and ankles when the swelling is sudden, severe, persistent, or accompanied by other concerning symptoms like pain, redness, warmth, or difficulty walking. Seek immediate medical attention if you experience these symptoms, especially if they are accompanied by shortness of breath, chest pain, or signs of infection.
snippet_highlighted_words: when the swelling is sudden, severe, persistent, or accompanied by other concerning symptoms like pain, redness, warmth, or difficulty walking

text_blocks.snippet: When to seek immediate medical attention:

list.title: Sudden or rapid swelling:
list.snippet: If the swelling appears suddenly and without a clear cause, it could indicate a blood clot or other serious issue.

list.title: Severe or persistent swelling:
list.snippet: Swelling that doesn't improve with rest or lifestyle changes, or that is accompanied by severe pain, needs prompt evaluation.

list.title: Swelling accompanied by other symptoms:
list.snippet: Shortness of breath, chest pain or tightness, fever, or a noticeable difference in swelling between legs could be signs of heart failure, infection, or a blood clot and require urgent care.

list.title: Difficulty walking or bearing weight:
list.snippet: Swelling that makes it difficult to walk or put weight on your foot or ankle could indicate a serious injury or other problem.

list.title: Painful swelling:
list.snippet: Painful swelling, especially if it's only on one leg, could be a sign of a blood clot or infection.

list.title: Persistent swelling:
list.snippet: If swelling lasts for more than a few days without improvement, it's best to consult with a doctor to rule out underlying conditions like kidney or heart issues.

list.title: Chronic swelling:
list.snippet: Swelling that occurs frequently or is a long-term issue may indicate a chronic condition requiring management.

list.title: Swelling accompanied by skin changes:
list.snippet: Redness, warmth, or discoloration of the swollen area could indicate an infection or other problem.

list.title: Swelling that doesn't respond to home care:
list.snippet: If self-care measures like elevation and compression don't help, consult your doctor.

text_blocks.snippet: Possible causes of swollen feet and ankles:

list.snippet: Blood clots (deep vein thrombosis - DVT): These can be life-threatening and require immediate medical attention.
Heart failure: Swelling, particularly in both legs, can be a sign of heart failure.
Kidney disease: Fluid retention due to kidney problems can lead to swelling.
Liver disease: Similar to kidney disease, liver problems can cause fluid buildup and swelling.
Infections: Infections in the foot or ankle can cause swelling, redness, and pain.
Injuries: Sprains, strains, or fractures can cause swelling and pain.
Chronic venous insufficiency: This condition affects blood flow back to the heart, causing fluid to pool in the legs and feet.
Medications: Certain medications can cause swelling as a side effect.
Pregnancy: Swelling is common during pregnancy, but excessive swelling should be monitored.
Gout: A type of arthritis that can cause sudden, painful swelling in the joints, especially the ankles.
Lymphedema: A condition where lymph fluid builds up in the tissues, causing swelling, usually in one or both legs.
